newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa's nuns carry on mission of mercy.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa's nuns carry on mission of mercy.

text.p: Mother Teresa's nuns on Tuesday pursued their works of charity among the poor in Calcutta with a prayer on their lips for their critically ill leader and her lifelong mission.

"We need these works of love more than the poor we practise them on," said Sister Dolores, who runs the Nirmal Hriday (Innocent Heart) home in the bustling Kalighat area of the eastern Indian city of Calcutta.
"We need them to transform our lives."
Sister Dolores is from the Missionaries of Charity, the religious order Mother Teresa founded in 1949 to take care of the poor, the sick and the terminally ill.
Today, it has more than 4,500 nuns who run over 450 homes in 111 countries, members of the order say.
Doctors on Tuesday said they were very concerned about Mother Teresa's health after she underwent heart surgery last week to clear two blocked arteries.
"She is still not out of danger, still critical," her team of doctors said in a medical bulletin.
The 86-year-old nun spent the weekend battling a longstanding lung problem and weak kidneys, as well as bronchial pneumonia.
At Nirmal Hrida care of themselves lay on pallets lining the walls of large rooms. Outside, traffic inched along narrow streets, crowded with hawkers, pedal rickshaws and stray cattle.
Dozens of nuns helped by volunteers distributed food to the 107 people who live in the two-storey home. Each got a banana, four slices of bread and a boiled egg -- the day's first meal.
"We're not a hospital. It's a home," said Sister Dolores when asked to name the most frequent diseases in the home.
"We look after them. We comfort them when they come here very ill or dying," she said. "Some get better and go away."
On a stretcher made of green cloth, wrapped on a metal frame and near the home's door, lay Kali Poda, mumbling to himself in delirium, a saline drip inserted in his right arm.
"Those closer to dying are brought up to the front," said one volunteer as he cradled the wizened Kali Poda in his arms.
A stretcher on the other side of the door bore a thin body bound in a tight white shroud.
In the women's ward nearby, Shakuntala sat eating her breakfast. "I've heard of Mother Teresa," she said. "I know she is ill. But God will save her. Otherwise, what will become of us?"
Located nearby is Prem Daan (Gift of Love), a home for the destitute run by Mother Teresa's nuns in a converted warehouse donated by a multinational chemical company.
There are 320 people living at the home, said Sister Denitza, who is in charge.
"We cook about 78 kg (172 lb) of rice, two large gunny sacks of potatoes and five or six baskets of vegetables to feed the poor at every meal," said one nun as she distributed food.
"It's very expensive. We do the shopping twice a week and bring back everything in an ambulance."
But the nun said the order did not worry about funds.
"The Lord will provide. If you work to help the poor, he will always provide," said the nun, who asked not to be named.
Mother Teresa's nuns run three other homes in Calcutta, for orphans, the mentally ill and leprosy patients. They prayed for her health as they went about their work.

Kneeling on the floor of the chapel in Prem Daan, one nun said: "Dearest Mary our Mother, we ask you to beg Jesus, your Son, to let Mother Teresa stay on. We need her among us. Keep her close to you in your heart, dear Jesus."
